## Short answer

MMR replaces "rank each document by its relevance to the query" with "rank each document by its *marginal* relevance — relevance minus redundancy with what has already been shown," using a single tunable knob λ. The formulation is well established and widely adopted; the *empirical* evidence that this particular similarity-based (implicit) form of diversification improves retrieval effectiveness is much weaker than its popularity suggests, and later TREC-based evaluations find it gives at best marginal, non-significant gains over a plain relevance baseline.

---

## 1. The mechanism (supported)

MMR was introduced by Jaime Carbonell and Jade Goldstein at SIGIR '98, "The use of MMR, diversity-based reranking for reordering documents and producing summaries," which "strives to reduce redundancy while maintaining query relevance in re-ranking retrieved documents and in selecting appropriate passages for text summarization" ([SIGIR'98 abstract](https://people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/sigir98/abstracts/carbonell.html)). A companion primary write-up appeared as Goldstein & Carbonell, TIPSTER Phase III Workshop, 1998 ([ACL Anthology X98-1025](https://aclanthology.org/X98-1025/)).

The criterion is a **linear combination of independently measured relevance and novelty**, applied greedily:

> MMR = argmax over dᵢ ∈ R\S of [ λ · Sim₁(dᵢ, q) − (1 − λ) · max over dⱼ ∈ S of Sim₂(dᵢ, dⱼ) ]

where R is the candidate set, S the already-selected documents, q the query ([arXiv:2407.04573, HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.04573)). λ ∈ [0,1] is the weighting factor: at λ = 1 MMR reduces to a standard relevance-ranked list; at λ = 0 it maximizes diversity among selected items ([arXiv:2407.04573](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.04573)).

Three properties follow directly from that formula (**inference**, not quoted claims):

- The novelty term uses **max** similarity to the selected set, not a sum or average. So MMR penalizes a document for being close to its *nearest* already-selected neighbor. It suppresses near-duplicates sharply but is comparatively insensitive to a result set that is broadly homogeneous without containing any close pair.
- Diversity is defined **relative to the result list**, not to query aspects or user intents. MMR has no model of *what* subtopics exist or how likely each is — a point later work makes explicit as the weakness of "implicit" diversification (see §3).
- The greedy, one-at-a-time construction means the output is an approximation to the set-level objective, not its optimum.

**Uncertain:** λ values recommended in the original text (a figure like "λ ≈ 0.3 for exploratory search, higher for focused search" circulates widely). I could not verify recommended values against the primary paper in this session — the CMU PDF of the SIGIR paper and the ACL Anthology PDF are both scanned image files with no extractable text layer, and the ACM Digital Library page returns 403. Treat any specific λ recommendation attributed to Carbonell & Goldstein as unverified here.

## 2. Evidence in the original paper (supported, but weak by modern standards)

The authors' own reported evidence was, in their words, preliminary and mostly qualitative:

- For **document reranking and single-document summarization**, "preliminary results indicate the benefits of MMR," with single-document results "borne out by" the SUMMAC-style summarization evaluation ([SIGIR'98 abstract](https://people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/sigir98/abstracts/carbonell.html)).
- The **clearest** benefit claimed is for non-redundant **multi-document summarization**, where "MMR results are clearly superior to non-MMR passage selection" ([SIGIR'98 abstract](https://people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/sigir98/abstracts/carbonell.html)).
- The retrieval evidence includes a **blind user preference study**: users were asked to find information from documents, told only that "method R" or "method S" had been used, and a majority preferred the MMR ordering as giving the broadest/most interesting topics (reported via [search-indexed summaries of the paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/243774776_The_use_of_mmr_and_diversity-based_reranking_in_document_reranking_and_summarization); I could not read the primary text directly, so the study's size and statistical treatment are unknown to me).

**Assessment (inference):** the strongest evidence in the founding paper is for *summarization*, not for search-result diversification. The retrieval evidence is a small preference study plus an unofficial trial-run evaluation — suggestive, not decisive.

## 3. Later evidence — and this is where it gets less favorable

**Framing and metrics.** Zhai, Cohen & Lafferty (SIGIR 2003) formalized *subtopic retrieval* — finding documents covering many subtopics of a topic — noting that here "the utility of a document in a ranking is dependent on other documents in the ranking, violating the assumption of independent relevance." They gave a probabilistic extension of MMR and introduced subtopic-recall-style metrics ([dblp record](https://dblp.org/rec/conf/sigir/ZhaiCL03.html); [Illinois Experts record](https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/beyond-independent-relevance-methods-and-evaluation-metrics-for-s/)). This is the paper that made MMR-style diversity *measurable*; I was unable to retrieve its full text (the UIUC host refused connection and the CMU mirror redirects), so I am not reporting its specific numbers.

**Head-to-head evaluation on TREC.** The most directly relevant negative evidence: on the TREC Web track diversity topics, MMR and MVA (novelty-based, implicit methods) show "at best marginal yet not significant improvements over the non-diversified ranking produced by DPH, even under training," with the largest observed improvement being **+3% (MVA's α-nDCG on the WT09 topics)** — results the authors say "corroborate observations regarding the lack of empirical validation of novelty-based approaches for diversifying Web search results" ([Santos, Macdonald & Ounis, *On the role of novelty for search result diversification*, Information Retrieval Journal](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10791-011-9180-x)). Note the source of this quotation is one of the xQuAD authors, i.e. a party with a stake in the comparison; the finding is nonetheless a controlled comparison on shared TREC data.

**Implicit vs. explicit.** Multiple comparative evaluations report that explicit, aspect-aware methods (xQuAD, PM-2) outperform MMR on all diversity measures, with MMR "least effective due to its simple predefined 'marginal relevance', which tries to capture novelty only based on inter-document similarity"; xQuAD instances took top performance in the TREC 2009 and 2010 Web track diversity tasks ([Santos et al., *Explicit web search result diversification*, Semantic Scholar](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/9b9c66bfb4cca231f38de8d6624c8dd674a3554f); [comparative study, U. Delaware](https://www.eecis.udel.edu/~hfang/pubs/ddr11.pdf)). A recent TOIS study likewise reports MMR yielding only marginal improvements over the retrieval baseline while xQuAD is significantly better on α#-nDCG at all depths ([*Diversification and Fairness in Search*, ACM TOIS](https://doi.org/10.1145/3774320)). **Caveat on access:** the Delaware PDF would not parse and the TOIS/Springer pages are gated; I am relying on indexed summaries for these two, so treat the exact wording as second-hand while the direction of the finding is consistent across all three sources.

**Computational side.** Jointly optimizing similarity and diversity is genuinely hard: the decision problem of vector retrieval under this objective is proved **NP-complete** (by reduction from k-subset-sum), and the authors note that the optimal λ "varies across scenarios and cannot be known a priori" ([arXiv:2407.04573](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.04573)). This supports the practical complaint that MMR's benefit is λ-dependent and its greedy solution is a heuristic.

## 4. What is disputed, and what is simply not well evidenced

- **Not disputed:** the formulation itself, the meaning of λ, and MMR's usefulness as a *redundancy filter* — e.g. in multi-document summarization, where the original paper's evidence was strongest ([SIGIR'98](https://people.eng.unimelb.edu.au/ammoffat/sigir98/abstracts/carbonell.html)), and in modern RAG/vector-store pipelines where it is a standard option ([OpenSearch docs](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/vector-search/specialized-operations/vector-search-mmr/), [Google Cloud Bigtable docs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/mmr-vector-search)). Those product docs establish adoption, not effectiveness.
- **Disputed / weakly supported:** that MMR improves *search result* quality on intent-diversity benchmarks. The TREC-based evidence points to marginal, statistically non-significant gains ([IRJ](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10791-011-9180-x)).
- **Genuine gap:** I found no primary study establishing a principled, transferable way to set λ; the literature I could reach explicitly says the optimum is scenario-dependent and unknowable in advance ([arXiv:2407.04573](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.04573)).
- **My own access limits:** the two most important primary texts (Carbonell & Goldstein 1998; Zhai et al. 2003) were not readable through my tools — scanned PDFs, a 403, a refused connection, and paywall redirects. Everything I attribute to them above comes from the SIGIR poster abstract, the ACL Anthology metadata, bibliographic records, or clearly-labeled indexed summaries. A definitive account of their internal numbers requires the actual PDFs.

**Bottom line (inference):** MMR is best understood as a *redundancy-removal* heuristic with a clean, cheap, interpretable knob — strong evidence for de-duplication and summarization, thin evidence as a search-diversification method compared to approaches that model query aspects explicitly.
